easy.heading: Warming Up With A Morning Brew
easy.body:
Starting today's easy puzzle was like taking that first sip of coffee—everything just clicked into place once I woke up. I began by looking at the constraint for cell 2,5 which had to be greater than five. Since the only number bigger than five in a domino set is six, I knew right away that cell was a six. That led me to look at its neighbor at 1,5 which was part of an equals region. It made sense to pair them up using one of the dominoes with a six in it. I settled on the 6,6 domino for that spot, which left me feeling pretty confident about the right side of the grid.

Next, I turned my attention to the top left. Cell 0,1 had a rule that it must be less than two, which really narrows things down. I tried out the 2,1 domino there, putting the one in that restricted spot. This worked out perfectly because it lined up with the equals region across the first column. Once those small numbers were out of the way, the middle section with the 3,3 or 2,2 dominoes became much clearer. It is always a relief when the easy puzzle lives up to its name and lets you build some momentum for the harder ones later on.

medium.heading: Squeezing Through The Middle Ground
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today from Rodolfo Kurchan really made me stop and think for a second. The layout had a few empty squares at 3,0 and 3,3 which act like roadblocks, forcing you to work around them. I found the best way in was focusing on the equals region at 3,1 and 3,2. Since those two had to be the same, I looked for a double domino and decided to use the 1,1 there. It felt like a safe bet and helped stabilize the bottom row while I figured out the rest of the board.

The trickiest part was definitely the cluster of equal cells at 1,3, 1,4, and 2,3. When you have three or more cells that all have to match, it really limits your domino choices. I had to play around with the 3,3 domino and the 2,4 domino to see how they would fit into the neighbors. I eventually realized that the less than two constraint at 0,3 was the key to the whole puzzle. By placing a one there, the rest of the dominoes like the 1,2 and 0,2 fell right into place like a game of Tetris. It was a nice little challenge that required a bit more foresight than the easy one.

hard.heading: Tackling The Big Grid Boss
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today was quite the marathon! With thirteen dominoes to place and a much larger grid, I really had to take my time. The breakthrough moment for me was noticing the massive equals regions near the bottom. Specifically, the block of four cells at 8,2, 8,3, 9,2, and 9,3 all had to be identical. That is a huge hint because it usually means you are looking for multiple dominoes with the same high or low values. I ended up using parts of the 6,6 and 5,6 dominoes to fill in those matching zones, which cleared up a lot of the visual clutter.

I did hit a bit of a dead end in the middle when I tried to force the 4,3 domino into the sum region of four. I realized that the sum rule at 1,2 and 2,2 was much easier to solve if I used the 1,2 domino itself or maybe a zero and a four. Once I corrected that mistake and worked through the empty squares that Rodolfo sprinkled throughout the center, the path to the finish line became clear. It felt great to finally connect the 0,0 and the 2,3 dominoes at the very end. This one definitely tested my patience, but the satisfaction of seeing all those constraints turn green was well worth the effort.

explanation.tips: Try to start with the most restrictive constraints first, like the less than or greater than boxes, because they usually only have one or two possible numbers. I also find it helpful to look for the empty squares early on since they tell you exactly where a domino cannot go. If you get stuck, look for equals regions that span across three or four cells, as those are usually the anchors that hold the whole solution together.
explanation.learned:
Today I learned how much empty squares can change the flow of a Pips puzzle. They really act as anchors that define the shape of the remaining dominoes. I also noticed that in the hard puzzle, the large blocks of equal cells are often the easiest way to start if you have double dominoes like 6,6 or 0,0 available.

Another fun takeaway was seeing how Ian Livengood and Rodolfo Kurchan have different styles. Ian's easy puzzle felt very linear and logical, while Rodolfo's medium and hard puzzles used more negative space to make you think about the geometry of the dominoes. It is cool to see how different designers approach the same set of rules.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle today?
faqs.answer: Start by identifying cells with specific limits, like less than or greater than constraints. Use the provided dominoes list to see which numbers are available and match them to the equals or sum regions on the board.

faqs.question: What does the equals region mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An equals region is a group of two or more cells that must all contain the same number of pips. This usually requires using doubles or matching ends of different dominoes.

faqs.question: Are there any tricks for the hard NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Focus on the largest regions first. In the hard version, look for sum constraints or large equal blocks as they narrow down your domino pool the fastest. Also, pay attention to the empty cells which act as borders.

faqs.question: Who created the NYT Pips puzzle for April 14 2026?
faqs.answer: The easy puzzle was constructed by Ian Livengood, and the medium and hard puzzles were designed by Rodolfo Kurchan.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must be placed either horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent cells, just like in a traditional game of dominoes.
